questions.q: How long is one day on Mars, and what is it called?
questions.do: Read the opening lines of What time is it on Mars?
questions.a: A Mars day is called a sol. It lasts 24 hours, 39 minutes and 35 seconds, about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day. That is why the rover clocks slowly drift against your watch.

questions.q: When is Mars next at its closest to Earth, and how long would a radio signal take to get there then?
questions.do: Press Next opposition under How far away is Mars? and read the Next opposition box.
questions.a: Opposition is on 19 Feb 2027 and the closest approach on 20 Feb 2027, about 101.4 million km away. A signal then takes about 5 minutes 38 seconds one way. This is the farthest 'close approach' of the whole 21st century.

questions.q: On what date is the Sun next directly between Earth and Mars, and why does that matter to the rover teams?
questions.do: Press Next conjunction and read the box, the readout Mars from Sun, in our sky, and the words under it.
questions.a: The next solar conjunction is on 21 Mar 2028. Mars is then on the far side of the Sun, about 357 million km away, and appears less than 3° from the Sun. The Sun's hot gas can scramble radio signals, so NASA stops sending commands for about two weeks.

questions.q: Which rover has been on Mars longer, and on what date did it land?
questions.do: Read the opening of Which sol, which season? and compare the two sol counters.
questions.a: Curiosity, which landed in Gale crater on 6 August 2012 (UTC). Perseverance landed in Jezero crater on 18 February 2021, so Curiosity's sol number is about 3,000 sols bigger.

questions.q: Mars years are numbered, like Earth years. When did Mars Year 1 begin, and when did Mars Year 39 begin?
questions.do: Read Which sol, which season?, then open How far to trust it and find the Mars Year 39 row.
questions.a: Mars Year 1 began on 11 April 1955, at the start of spring in Mars's northern half. Mars Year 39 began on 30 September 2026 (08:16 UTC by ESA's count; this page gets 08:22).
